meta.name: Hypoglycemic Altered Mental Status — 'He Just Isn't Acting Right': BLS Scope — Oral Glucose Withheld, Glucagon 1 mg IM

patient.name: John Harris
patient.chiefComplaint: Confused and 'not acting right' for the past hour per his wife — mumbling incoherently, pale and sweaty, unable to answer questions.

history.hpi: 68-year-old male with Type 2 diabetes and hypertension. He was fine this morning and ate breakfast around 08:00. He took his morning medications as always and spent the day working in the garage, completely skipping lunch. About an hour ago (~14:00) he came inside looking pale and sweaty, confused, and 'just not making any sense.' His wife has not been able to get him to answer her since. It is now almost 15:00. His long-acting Lantus insulin is taken every night before bed; his oral metformin was taken this morning. No trauma, no witnessed seizure activity, no complaints voiced before the confusion began.
medications: Metformin (oral, for diabetes) — taken this morning
Lisinopril (for blood pressure) — taken this morning
Lantus (insulin glargine, long-acting) — one shot every night before bed
history.lastOralIntake: Breakfast around 8 AM. He completely skipped lunch while working in the garage — it is now almost 3 PM.
history.events: Nothing unusual per his wife: 'He took his morning medications as always. He was working in the garage and just came inside about an hour ago looking like this.' She could not get him to answer her and called 911.

scene.dispatch: Medic 1, respond to 123 Maple Street for a 68-year-old male, reported to be 'acting strangely.' The patient's wife is on scene. Time out is 14:32.
scene.location: Living room of a clean, well-kept single-family home at 123 Maple Street. The patient is sitting slumped in a recliner.
scene.safety: Scene is a clean, well-kept single-family home with no immediate hazards. Standard BSI. An anxious woman in her 60s meets the crew at the door and leads them to the living room.
scene.bystanders: Wife, Mary — the primary and ONLY reliable historian; the patient cannot answer questions reliably. She reports: 'Thank you for coming so quickly! It's my husband, John. He just isn't acting right. He was fine this morning, but for the last hour, he's been confused and just isn't making any sense. I can't get him to answer me.'
visualCues: Elderly male sitting slumped in a recliner, eyes open but gaze unfocused — does not track the crew
Anxious, very worried wife standing next to the recliner
Clean, tidy living room — no pill bottles, alcohol, or paraphernalia in view, no signs of trauma

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: A 68-year-old diabetic on nightly Lantus and morning metformin skipped lunch and has been 'not acting right' for an hour. He mumbles incoherently, does not track the providers, is A&Ox0, and will not follow commands — but his airway is patent, his breathing adequate, and his radial pulse strong. The wife is the entire history: the patient cannot give one, and her SAMPLE points straight at the answer — insulin plus metformin plus a skipped meal. The single scenario-defining action is putting a glucometer on him: BGL is 45 mg/dL. From there the BLS treatment decision is the teaching point. Oral glucose is out — MATC reserves it for a conscious patient with a patent airway, and a man who cannot follow commands cannot safely swallow; putting gel in his mouth is a safety failure, not a treatment. IV dextrose — MATC's definitive therapy for the patient who cannot protect his own airway — is not available to this crew: they have not taken pharmacology and cannot establish IV access. The protocol's own language resolves the impasse: glucagon IM/IN is 'an option for patients for whom IV access cannot be established,' which is definitionally true of a BLS crew. Adult dose is a fixed 1 mg IM/IN. The pale, cool, diaphoretic skin is the protocol's own pertinent finding — diaphoresis may be associated with hypoglycemia — and the heart rate of 112 is the catecholamine response to a starving brain.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent and self-maintained. No audible stridor or gurgling — but he will not follow commands and cannot safely swallow; oral glucose is not an option
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Respirations slightly fast (RR 20) but of adequate depth, unlabored; lungs clear bilaterally
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse present, rapid, and strong at 112; no obvious major bleeding; skin pale, cool, and diaphoretic (clammy)
clinicalPresentation.pupils: 4 mm, PERRL (equal, round, reactive to light)
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Does not follow commands; moves all four extremities spontaneously; localizes; no focal deficit appreciated
otherFindings: BLOOD GLUCOSE 45 mg/dL — but ONLY if the crew thinks to check it
A&Ox0 — responds to verbal stimuli with incomprehensible mumbling; does not track providers with his eyes
Diabetic on insulin (nightly Lantus) + metformin who SKIPPED LUNCH — the wife's SAMPLE history is the whole mechanism
MATC: diaphoresis may be associated with hypoglycemia — the pale, cool, clammy skin is a protocol-listed finding
Cannot follow commands = cannot safely swallow = oral glucose is contraindicated

IV dextrose is the definitive ALS therapy but this BLS crew cannot establish IV access — MATC's glucagon clause ('for patients for whom IV access cannot be established') therefore applies: glucagon 1 mg IM/IN
No insulin pump present — Lantus is given by nightly injection
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (incomprehensible mumbling — does not answer questions, does not track the providers)

expectedActions.shortAction: Primary survey — with depressed mental status, airway protection and ventilation come first
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Altered Mental Status Patient Safety 1 — the initial focus in any depressed mental status is airway, oxygenation, ventilation, and perfusion. His airway is patent and self-maintained NOW; the primary survey establishes the baseline the crew will measure deterioration against.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: With depressed mental status, initial focus is on airway protection, oxygenation, ventilation, and perfusion.

expectedActions.shortAction: Take the SAMPLE history from the wife — the patient cannot give one
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Altered Mental Status Key Consideration 1 — history from bystanders and caregivers. Mary is the only reliable historian on this scene, and her answers (insulin + metformin, skipped lunch, gradual onset over an hour) contain the entire diagnosis. A crew that only questions the mumbling patient learns nothing.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Key Considerations: History from bystanders and caregivers. Key Documentation Elements: Baseline developmental status and change from baseline.

expectedActions.shortAction: CHECK BLOOD GLUCOSE — AMS + diabetic history makes the glucometer mandatory
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Hypoglycemia Inclusion Criteria 2 and 5 — altered level of consciousness, and history of diabetes with other medical symptoms — both put this patient squarely in the protocol, and the Assessment's first line is to check a blood glucose. The stated performance measure is that a glucose is checked on ALL patients with altered level of consciousness. 'Not acting right' = check the sugar. Result: 45 mg/dL.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Inclusion Criteria: Patients with altered level of consciousness. Patients with history of diabetes and other medical symptoms. Assessment: Monitoring: Check blood glucose level. Performance Measures: When in scope of practice, blood glucose is checked for all patients with symptoms of altered level of consciousness, seizure, stroke, or hypoglycemia.

expectedActions.shortAction: Run the AEIOU-TIPS differential — 'I' for Insulin fits the history
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Altered Mental Status Key Consideration 4 — the structured differential keeps the crew from guessing. Stroke, overdose, infection, and seizure are all live possibilities in a confused 68-year-old until the exam and the glucometer rule them out; the SAMPLE history makes Insulin (hypoglycemia) the front-runner.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider the following differential using the mnemonic AEIOU-TIPS: A – Alcohol, Abuse, Atypical migraine; E – Epilepsy, Electrolytes; I – Insulin (hypoglycemia); O – Oxygen, Overdose; U – Uremia (kidney failure); T – Trauma, Tumor; I – Infection; P – Psych, Poisoning; S – Seizure, Subarachnoid hemorrhage, Sepsis.

expectedActions.shortAction: Full AMS workup: GCS, pupils, stroke screen, SpO2, skin temperature, environment sweep
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Altered Mental Status Assessment — the systematic sweep for treatable causes, every element of it within BLS scope. Pupils 4 mm PERRL, no focal deficit, no trauma, no fever, unremarkable environment — every negative finding sharpens the hypoglycemia diagnosis the glucometer confirms.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Look for treatable causes of altered mental status (AMS): Airway: Make sure airway remains patent; reposition patient as needed. Breathing: Look for respiratory depression; check SPO2, EtCO2, and CO detector readings. Circulation: Look for signs of poor perfusion. Glasgow Coma Score and/or AVPU. Pupils. Stroke assessment tool including focal neurologic findings. Blood glucose level. Extremities/skin: Track marks, hydration, edema, dialysis shunt, temperature to touch (or if able, use a thermometer), signs of trauma. Environment: Survey for pills, paraphernalia, substance use, medication patches, medical devices.

expectedActions.shortAction: WITHHOLD oral glucose — reserved for a conscious patient with a patent airway; he cannot safely swallow
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Hypoglycemia Treatment 2a — oral glucose (25 g adult) is authorized ONLY for the conscious patient with a patent airway. A man who is A&Ox0, mumbling, and unable to follow commands cannot protect against aspiration. Putting gel in his mouth is a safety failure, not a treatment. The protocol routes him to Treatment 2b instead.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If blood glucose is 60 mg/dL or less administer one of the following: Conscious patient with a patent airway: Glucose, oral (in form of glucose tablets, glucose gel, tube of cake icing, etc.): Adult Dosing: 25 g; Pediatric Dosing: 0.5–1 g/kg.

expectedActions.shortAction: Glucagon 1 mg IM/IN (adult fixed dose) — a BLS crew cannot establish IV access
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Hypoglycemia Treatment 2b — for the patient who cannot protect his own airway, dextrose IV is MATC's definitive treatment, but it requires vascular access this pre-pharmacology crew cannot establish. The protocol's own language resolves it: glucagon IM/IN is 'an option for patients for whom IV access cannot be established' — definitionally true of a BLS crew. Fixed adult dose 1 mg IM/IN. Glucagon mobilizes hepatic glycogen rather than delivering glucose, so onset is slower than IV dextrose — which is exactly why the reassessment and repeat glucose that follow are mandatory.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If blood glucose is 60 mg/dL or less administer one of the following: Unconscious patient, or patients who are unable to protect their own airway: Glucagon IM/IN – an option for patients for whom IV access cannot be established: Adult dosing: 1 mg IM/IN (or prefilled 3 mg dry powder IN or prefilled IM autoinjector).

expectedActions.shortAction: Secondary survey: confirm no insulin pump; note metformin's possible contribution
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Hypoglycemia Assessment 2 — the hypoglycemia-specific secondary survey starts with a search for an automated insulin delivery device. John's Lantus comes by nightly injection and there is no pump to disable, but the crew should confirm that with their hands, not the wife's word alone. Key Consideration 2 adds the oral agents to the picture.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Secondary survey pertinent to altered blood glucose level: Evaluate for presence of an automated external insulin delivery device (insulin pump). Constitutional: assess for tachycardia and hypotension. Neurologic: Assess GCS and mental status. Assess for focal neurologic deficit: motor and sensory. Key Considerations: Consider contribution of oral diabetic medications to hypoglycemia.

transitions.if: BGL checked; glucagon 1 mg IM given
transitions.condition: Crew checks the blood glucose (45 mg/dL), correctly withholds oral glucose in a patient who cannot safely swallow, and — with IV dextrose unavailable at BLS scope — administers glucagon 1 mg IM/IN under the protocol's clause for patients for whom IV access cannot be established.

Crew fails to check a blood glucose, fails to recognize the signs of hypoglycemia, or attempts to force oral glucose on a confused patient who cannot safely swallow (an immediate safety failure). The untreated blood sugar continues to fall and the patient deteriorates over approximately 10 minutes.

phases.name: Glucagon given
phases.description: Glucagon works the way its mechanism promises — slowly. It does not deliver glucose; it asks the liver to release stored glycogen, so the first minutes after the injection change nothing, and the airway watch continues: a hypoglycemic patient who has not yet turned the corner can still lose his airway, and oral glucose remains contraindicated until he can follow commands. Then the mumbling organizes into words; he begins looking at the providers and can state his name. Within 15 minutes he is Alert and Oriented ×4, asking 'Wow, I feel a little shaky. What happened?' Repeat glucose during the recovery reads 110 mg/dL; the skin turns pink, warm, and dry; and the heart rate settles to 88. Two protocol details matter here. First, reassessment is a named protocol step, not a courtesy: vitals, mental status, and — because his mentation had not yet normalized when it was drawn — the repeat glucose. Once his mental status has returned to normal, the protocol is equally explicit that further glucose checks are NOT required. Second, what glucagon spent cannot be spent twice: his hepatic glycogen stores are now partly emptied, and the nightly basal Lantus dose is still ahead of him — facts that belong in the disposition conversation coming next. Document what was found, what was given, and what changed.
phases.triggerCondition: Blood glucose 45 mg/dL identified, oral glucose correctly withheld, and glucagon 1 mg IM/IN administered under the protocol's no-IV-access clause. Glucagon mobilizes hepatic glycogen, so the response is slower than IV dextrose: over ~15 minutes mental status returns to Alert and Oriented ×4; repeat glucose 110 mg/dL.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent and self-maintained; speech clear and appropriate
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse strong and regular at 88; skin pink, warm, and dry
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Follows commands; moves all four extremities purposefully; no focal deficit
otherFindings: Alert and Oriented ×4 within 15 minutes of glucagon — can state his name, location, date, and events
Repeat glucose 110 mg/dL — drawn during recovery, before mentation fully normalized
Protocol: once mental status has returned to normal, further repeat glucose checks are NOT necessary
Glucagon mobilized hepatic glycogen rather than delivering glucose — the recovery was slower than IV dextrose, and those stores are now partly spent
He is now a competent adult — the disposition conversation is coming, and MATC answers it with an 8-item checklist
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Wow, I feel a little shaky. What happened?

expectedActions.shortAction: Guard the airway while glucagon takes effect — position, suction staged, continuous watch
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Altered Mental Status Patient Safety 1 — with depressed mental status the initial focus stays on airway protection, oxygenation, ventilation, and perfusion. Glucagon's slower onset means minutes in which the airway can still be lost; the watch does not end until he is following commands.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: With depressed mental status, initial focus is on airway protection, oxygenation, ventilation, and perfusion.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vitals and mental status; repeat BGL only while mentation is not yet normal
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Hypoglycemia Treatment 3 — reassessment after treatment is a named protocol step: vitals, neuro status, and mental status. Glucagon's slower mechanism makes this reassessment the only evidence of whether the treatment is working. The repeat glucose (110 mg/dL) belongs to the window before mentation normalizes; once he is A&Ox4, the protocol explicitly says another stick is not necessary.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Reassess patient: Reassess vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment) and mental status. Repeat check of blood glucose level if previous hypoglycemia and mental status has not returned to normal. It is not necessary to repeat check of blood glucose level blood sugar if mental status has returned to normal.

expectedActions.shortAction: Document the POC glucose values and the reassessment after glucagon
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Hypoglycemia Key Documentation Elements — the point-of-care glucose and the post-glucagon reassessment of vitals and mental status are the required record of this call. If the disposition ends in a release, this documentation carries the encounter.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Key Documentation Elements: Document reassessment of vital signs and mental status after administration of glucose/dextrose/glucagon. Document point of care glucose level (if in scope of practice) when indicated.

transitions.condition: Reassessment confirms sustained normal mental status (A&Ox4), stable vitals, and repeat glucose 110 mg/dL. The crew must now work the disposition decision with a recovered, competent adult using MATC's 8-item release-without-transport checklist — with glucagon's slower, glycogen-dependent mechanism weighing on the crew-agreement half of criterion (v).

phases.name: Recovery confirmed
phases.description: John is fully recovered, mildly embarrassed, and hungry. Mary offers to make him a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, and he asks whether he really has to go to the hospital. MATC does not leave this to gut feel — it gives an 8-item checklist, release without transport only if ALL are true. Walk it literally: (i) repeat glucose 110 is greater than 80 — pass. (ii) He takes insulin and metformin and does NOT take long-acting oral sulfonylureas — read the words carefully: the criterion excludes glipizide/glyburide-class agents, not long-acting insulin, so Lantus PASSES this criterion as written. (iii) Normal mental status, no focal deficits — pass. (iv) He can promptly obtain and will eat a carbohydrate meal — the PB&J, pass. (vi) A reliable adult (Mary) will stay with him — pass. (vii) No major co-morbid symptoms — no chest pain, dyspnea, seizure, or intoxication — pass. (viii) Clear cause identified — a missed meal, the protocol's own example — pass. Everything therefore hinges on (v): the patient must REFUSE transport AND the EMS clinicians must AGREE transport is not indicated. Offer transport first. If he accepts, he goes. If he refuses, the protocol permits release — and criterion (v) is exactly where the crew's judgment belongs: this recovery was bought with glucagon, which spent hepatic glycogen stores he cannot instantly replace, and the nightly basal Lantus dose is still ahead of him. The source curriculum is explicit that he should be strongly encouraged to accept transport because the glucagon may wear off. Whatever is decided, the performance measure is blunt: if released at scene, the criteria are documented.
phases.triggerCondition: Reassessment confirms sustained recovery: A&Ox4, stable vitals, repeat glucose 110 mg/dL. The patient is again a competent adult, and the crew must resolve disposition per the MATC release-without-transport criteria.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent and self-maintained; speaking in full sentences
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse strong and regular at 84; skin pink, warm, and dry
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Normal; follows all commands; steady when repositioned; no focal deficit
otherFindings: RELEASE CHECKLIST, applied literally: passes (i) glucose 110 > 80; (ii) insulin + metformin, NO oral sulfonylureas; (iii) normal mentation, no deficits; (iv) will eat a carb meal; (vi) reliable adult staying; (vii) no major co-morbid symptoms; (viii) clear cause — missed meal
Criterion (ii) excludes long-acting ORAL SULFONYLUREAS — Lantus is long-acting INSULIN and passes the criterion as written
The entire disposition hinges on criterion (v): patient refuses transport AND EMS clinicians agree transport not indicated
Offer transport first — if he accepts, he goes; refusal is his to make, not Mary's
Crew judgment inside 'EMS clinicians agree': glucagon spent his glycogen stores, its effect may wear off, and tonight's basal Lantus dose is still ahead of him — strong grounds to encourage transport
Performance measure: if released at scene, criteria documented for safe release
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Honestly, I feel fine now — just a little shaky. Mary's making me a sandwich. Do I really need to go in?

expectedActions.shortAction: Walk ALL 8 release criteria literally — he passes i–iv and vi–viii; everything hinges on v
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Hypoglycemia Disposition 4c — release without transport may be considered only if ALL eight criteria are true. Applied as written, John passes seven of the eight: note that criterion ii excludes long-acting ORAL sulfonylureas (glipizide/glyburide class), not long-acting insulin — his Lantus + metformin regimen satisfies it. The remaining criterion, v, requires the patient to refuse AND the crew to agree transport is not indicated. The protocol replaces the argument with a checklist.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If symptoms of hypoglycemia resolve after treatment, release without transport should only be considered if all the following are true: Repeat glucose is greater than 80 mg/dL; Patient takes insulin or metformin to control diabetes and does not take long-acting oral sulphunylurea agents (e.g., glipizide, glyburide, or others); Patient returns to normal mental status, with no focal neurologic signs/symptoms after receiving glucose/dextrose; Patient can promptly obtain and will eat a carbohydrate meal; Patient or legal guardian refuses transport and EMS clinicians agree transport not indicated; A reliable adult will be staying with patient; No major co-morbid symptoms exist, like chest pain, shortness of breath, seizures, intoxication; A clear cause of the hypoglycemia is identified (e.g., missed meal).

expectedActions.shortAction: Have him promptly eat a carbohydrate meal (the PB&J) — a required release criterion
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Hypoglycemia Disposition 4c-iv — release is only on the table if the patient can promptly obtain and will eat a carbohydrate meal. Glucagon corrected the number by emptying hepatic glycogen stores; the meal is what replenishes them against the basal insulin still working in the background — after glucagon, the carbohydrate meal is even more load-bearing than it would be after IV dextrose.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Release without transport should only be considered if all the following are true: Patient can promptly obtain and will eat a carbohydrate meal. A clear cause of the hypoglycemia is identified (e.g., missed meal).

expectedActions.shortAction: Offer transport — release requires HIS refusal plus crew agreement; if he accepts, he goes
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Hypoglycemia Disposition 4c-v — the release pathway requires that the patient or legal guardian refuses transport AND the EMS clinicians agree transport is not indicated. Both halves matter: John (not Mary) owns the refusal now that his capacity has returned, and the crew's clinical judgment is the second lock on the gate — glucagon's effect may wear off as the spent glycogen runs out, and the nightly Lantus dose is still ahead of him, which is why he should be strongly encouraged to accept transport. If either half of criterion v is missing, he is transported.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Release without transport should only be considered if all the following are true: Patient or legal guardian refuses transport and EMS clinicians agree transport not indicated. Disposition: If hypoglycemia with continued symptoms, transport to closest appropriate receiving facility.

expectedActions.shortAction: Document every release criterion if he stays; document the reassessment either way
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Hypoglycemia Performance Measures — if the patient is released at scene, the criteria for safe release are documented. Combined with the documented glucose values and post-glucagon reassessment, this is the complete record the protocol demands of a treat-and-release hypoglycemia call.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Performance Measures: If patient released at scene, criteria documented for safe release. Key Documentation Elements: Document reassessment of vital signs and mental status after administration of glucose/dextrose/glucagon. Document point of care glucose level (if in scope of practice) when indicated.

phases.name: BGL never checked
phases.description: The crew never put a glucometer on him — or worse, tried to force oral glucose into a confused man who cannot swallow. Ten minutes later the mumbling has stopped, and not because he improved: he now responds only to a sternal rub with a groan. The untreated sugar has fallen to 30 mg/dL, his respirations have slowed to 10 and gone shallow, his pressure is drifting down at 102/64, and the pulse is 124 and thready. He is at high risk for a seizure, and the quiet patient is the emergency the loud one never was. The rescue now runs through the MATC airway ladder BEFORE the sugar — and every rung of it is BLS: open and maintain the airway with positioning, suction ready, an adjunct sized to his reflexes (NPA while a gag persists, OPA if it is gone), oxygen titrated to 94–98%, and BVM support of his inadequate spontaneous respirations at the protocol's adult rate. Only with the airway and ventilation held does the crew get the glucose it owed him ten minutes ago: check the BGL (30 mg/dL) and give glucagon 1 mg IM/IN — oral glucose is absolutely contraindicated at this level of consciousness, and IV dextrose is out of reach at BLS scope. This patient is critical and transports emergently; dextrose remains the definitive therapy he will get from an intercepting ALS unit or the emergency department. The debrief writes itself: 'not acting right' = check the sugar, and a BGL is a vital sign in every AMS patient.
phases.triggerCondition: Blood glucose was never checked and no glucose was given (or oral glucose was inappropriately attempted). Approximately 10 minutes after initial contact the untreated hypoglycemia deepens: he stops mumbling, responds only to painful stimuli with a groan, respirations slow to 10 and shallow, and he is at high risk for seizure.

clinicalPresentation.airway: At risk — decreasing muscle tone, sonorous respirations developing when his head lolls back; no active vomiting; suction must be staged
clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 10 and SHALLOW — inadequate minute ventilation; SpO2 drifting down, EtCO2 rising
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Pulse 124 and THREADY; BP drifting down at 102/64; skin increasingly pale and very clammy
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Responds to sternal rub with a groan and withdrawal; no purposeful movement; no longer mumbling
otherFindings: GLUCOSE 30 mg/dL — the number nobody looked for
The mumbling stopping was NOT improvement — it was deterioration
High risk for seizure — untreated hypoglycemic decompensation
RR 10 and shallow = hypoventilation: support spontaneous respirations with BVM per MATC airway protocol
RESCUE ORDER: airway and ventilation FIRST, then BGL, then glucagon 1 mg IM/IN — no IV rescue exists at BLS scope
Oral glucose is absolutely contraindicated — he is responsive to pain only
This patient is now critical: rapid transport to prevent permanent brain injury or death

expectedActions.shortAction: Open and maintain the airway — position, suction ready, NPA/OPA as tolerated
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Airway Management Treatment 3 — head tilt/chin lift, suction, and an adjunct sized to his reflexes: NPA while a gag persists, OPA if it is gone. His falling tone and developing sonorous respirations make the airway the first problem to solve; positioning alone may clear it.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Open and maintain patent airway. If needed, Provide head tilt/chin lift, or jaw thrust if concern for potential spinal injury. Suction airway. Oropharyngeal airways (OPA) or nasopharyngeal airways (NPA) can be placed if needed to maintain a patent airway and make BVM ventilation more effective: OPA are used for patients without gag reflex; NPA are used for patients with gag reflex.

expectedActions.shortAction: BVM-assist his spontaneous respirations — RR 10 and shallow is hypoventilation
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Airway Management Treatment 4 and BVM notes — respiratory failure gets BVM ventilation, two-person two-thumbs-up preferred, and the hypoventilating adult gets his spontaneous respirations SUPPORTED rather than replaced. EtCO2 52 and climbing with SpO2 91 is the protocol's picture of inadequate minute ventilation.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Use bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation in the setting of respiratory failure or arrest. Two-person, two-thumbs-up BVM ventilation is preferred. Rate: Adult: 10–12 breaths/minute. Ventilation rate — Adult: Support spontaneous respirations if the patient is hypoventilating.

expectedActions.shortAction: Oxygen titrated to SpO2 94–98% with continuous pulse oximetry
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Airway Management Treatment 2 and Monitoring 2 — oxygen is titrated to the 94–98% target, delivered by whatever the presentation demands (here, the BVM), with pulse oximetry tracking oxygenation throughout the rescue.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer oxygen if needed for air hunger or respiratory distress and titrate to a target SPO2 of 94–98%. Depending on patient presentation, this may be accomplished with nasal cannula, nonrebreather, BVM, NIV. Pulse oximetry is indicated to assess oxygenation.

expectedActions.shortAction: Check the blood glucose NOW — the vital sign owed 10 minutes ago (reads 30 mg/dL)
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Altered Mental Status Assessment 9 and Performance Measures — the blood glucose is a mandatory element of the AMS workup, and the protocol's stated measure of success is that hypoglycemia was considered and a glucose obtained. Nothing in this branch improves until this number is on the screen.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Look for treatable causes of altered mental status (AMS): Blood glucose level. Performance Measures: Hypoglycemia considered and treated appropriately - Blood glucose level obtained.

expectedActions.shortAction: Glucagon 1 mg IM/IN — pain-responsive, cannot swallow; no IV option at BLS scope
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Hypoglycemia Treatment 2b — a pain-responsive patient cannot protect his own airway, so oral glucose is absolutely contraindicated, and this crew cannot establish the IV access that dextrose requires. The protocol's glucagon clause — 'an option for patients for whom IV access cannot be established' — is the one treatment rung available: fixed adult dose 1 mg IM/IN, given while the airway and ventilation are held.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If blood glucose is 60 mg/dL or less administer one of the following: Unconscious patient, or patients who are unable to protect their own airway: Glucagon IM/IN – an option for patients for whom IV access cannot be established: Adult dosing: 1 mg IM/IN (or prefilled 3 mg dry powder IN or prefilled IM autoinjector).

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess and transport emergently — this patient is critical and is not a release candidate
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Hypoglycemia Treatment 3 and Disposition 4a — reassess vitals and mental status after treatment, repeat the glucose while mentation remains abnormal, and transport hypoglycemia with continued symptoms to the closest appropriate receiving facility. A patient who decompensated to pain-responsive in the crew's presence goes to the hospital regardless of how well the glucagon works — dextrose remains the definitive therapy he will get from an intercepting ALS unit or the emergency department.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Reassess patient: Reassess vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment) and mental status. Repeat check of blood glucose level if previous hypoglycemia and mental status has not returned to normal. Disposition: If hypoglycemia with continued symptoms, transport to closest appropriate receiving facility.
